references.name: Gary Gorton & K. Geert Rouwenhorst
references.desc:
Yale economists; "Facts and Fantasies About Commodity Futures"
      (2004)
references.connection:
Provided the academic foundation Rogers had been seeking —
      commodity futures have returned more than equities with less risk
      over 43 years; futures outperformed matching company stocks 3x.

references.name: King Hubbert
references.desc:
Shell Oil geologist; "Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels"
      (1956)
references.connection:
Predicted U.S. oil production would peak by early 1970s —
      exactly correct. Rogers uses his framework to argue world peak
      is imminent.

references.name: Matthew Simmons
references.desc: Houston investment banker; energy adviser to George W. Bush
references.connection:
Based on reading hundreds of geological reports, concluded
      Saudi Arabia's major fields are peaking and Ghawar is 90%
      depleted — the most alarming supply-side argument in the book.

references.name: T. Boone Pickens
references.connection:
Quoted: "We'll never be flush with oil again. The worldwide
      decline will be so steep that whatever we put back will never
      allow us to catch up."

references.name: Daniel Yergin
references.desc: Cambridge Energy Research Associates; author of "The Prize"
references.connection:
Represents the optimist view — digital oil fields will extend
      reserves. Rogers notes Yergin predicted oil prices would fall
      in 2003, just before they doubled in 28 months.

references.name: Barry Bannister
references.connection:
Documented the 130-year alternating cycles of stocks and
      commodities, averaging 18 years each — the historical foundation
      of Rogers's timing thesis.

references.name: Colin Campbell
references.connection:
Applied Hubbert's method globally; predicted worldwide oil
      production peak around 2005.

references.name: CRB Commodity Yearbook
references.connection:
Rogers's primary research tool since 1971 — the source he
      returned to in 1998 when he spotted the commodity bull.

references.name: George Soros
references.connection:
Rogers's partner from 1968–1980; the fund reportedly returned
      4,200% while the S&P 500 returned 47%.

references.name: Bernard Baruch
references.connection:
The shoeshine boy anecdote — Baruch sold everything when his
      shoeshine man started giving stock tips in the 1920s. Rogers uses
      it as the archetype for recognizing market hysteria.
